tldr: OSCAR is a generalist agent that autonomously controls desktop and mobile OS environments by translating user instructions into executable Python code, using state-aware reasoning, GUI grounding, and task-driven re-planning to adapt to real-time feedback.
contributions: A generalist OS control agent (OSCAR) that uses standardized mouse/keyboard inputs and screen image processing to interact across diverse desktop and mobile applications
A dual-grounding observation approach combining Set-of-Mark (SoM) visual prompts with semantic labels extracted from OS Accessibility trees
A state machine architecture with error-handling mechanisms and task-driven re-planning for adaptive execution
Strong performance across GAIA, OSWorld, and AndroidWorld benchmarks
methods: OSCAR operates as a state machine cycling through Init, Observe, Plan, Execute, and Verify states. It captures screenshots and enhances GUI understanding via dual grounding: visual grounding using SoM prompts derived from OS Accessibility tree coordinates, and semantic grounding by adding descriptive element labels. The agent translates instructions into executable Python code using PyAutoGUI for mouse/keyboard control. Task-driven re-planning decomposes instructions into sub-tasks via standardized operating procedures, enabling fine-grained re-planning of specific tasks rather than full workflow replanning when verification fails.
results: On GAIA benchmark, OSCAR achieved 28.7% average success rate, with 13.5% on Level 3 tasks (nearly doubling MMAC's 6.1%). On OSWorld, it achieved 24.5% success rate. On AndroidWorld, it achieved 61.6% success rate. OSCAR outperformed all baselines across desktop and mobile benchmarks.
limitations: The paper notes that previous static-environment methods fail when agents deviate from predetermined action sequences, highlighting that without real-time feedback and adaptive adjustment, agents struggle in real-world scenarios. The approach may also face challenges with critical system exceptions such as local model backend failures or excessive open files/processes, requiring user intervention.
